newsitem.title: FRANCE: Defeated French right blames Juppe, Chirac aides.
newsitem.headline: Defeated French right blames Juppe, Chirac aides.

text.p: War raged in the defeated French right on Wednesday as vengeful rivals sought to oust ex-prime minister Alain Juppe from the Gaullist party leadership.

Pierre Mazeaud, chairman of the outgoing National Assembly's legal committee, blamed top aides of conservative President Jacques Chirac for convincing him to call a snap election which backfired disastrously with a left-wing rout on Sunday.
"(Chirac) must ask himself questions about his aides...It is high time to draw the conclusions from this failure, and for everyone to take the consequences," Mazeaud said.

"The five who led Chirac astray," the tabloid Le Parisien said in a banner headline, adding pictures of Chirac's three closest aides, including his own daughter Claude, the president's powerful public relations adviser.

Also singled out were the secretary-general of the Elysee presidential palace, Dominique de Villepin, and Chirac's media adviser Claude Pilhan, Juppe and his chief of staff, diplomat Maurice Gourdault-Montague.

Juppe, portrayed by the popular daily France-Soir as the martyred Saint Sebastian riddled with arrows, faced a rebellion by fellow-Gaullists backing his rival Philippe Seguin for the leadership of their Rally for the Republic (RPR) party.
"In every democratic party in the world, a leader who has led a campaign to a major failure resigns," former interior minister Charles Pasqua told France Inter radio.

"It is clear he cannot lead our movement back to victory. Only Seguin can, since he embodies the potential for our movement to rediscover its roots in the people and he has a certain dynamism and charisma," Pasqua said.
Seguin, the former National Assembly speaker, took over the leadership of the right's election campaign at the last minute after Juppe bowed out following the first-round left-wing upset.
Mazeaud said Juppe, who is resisting attempts to oust him from the party leadership, should make his own decision to go. "It would enhance his image with activists and voters," he said.
Playing for time to weather the storm, Juppe has proposed holding an RPR congress in September to elect a new leader, a suggestion his foes branded unacceptable.

Outgoing interior minister Jean-Louis Debre, whom Juppe appointed RPR secretary-general on Tuesday, called for a halt in the Juppe-Seguin rivalry which he described as a ferocious fight aimed at jockeying for power for presidential elections.
"I hope everyone will display dignity and restraint...We must let our members speak up. This is what a democratic movement is about," Debre said.
The election makes Chirac a virtual prisoner of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin with five years left of his seven-year presidential term.

One of Chirac's closest friends, write Denis Tillinac, published a withering attack on Juppe, Villepin and their aides in the newspaper Le Monde, saying they had led the president away from his campaign promises, cut him off from the "real country" and stampeded him into the disastrous dissolution.
"Worse still, they never stopped committing Chirac to Juppe's rescue...A president is not a megaphone for his prime minister, even if his voice carries further," Tillinac wrote.

Juppe did not spell out if he would be a candidate to keep the party leadership, but he made clear he had no intention of yielding to growing calls from backers of Seguin, a left-wing Gaullist, for his immediate resignation.
The RPR's centre-right partner, the Union for French Democracy (UDF), seemed initially to be managing its post-defeat power struggle more harmoniously.

UDF leader Francois Leotard said he would stand down as head of the Republican Party this month, clearing the way for ex-finance minister Alain Madelin to take over the party which he had threatened to split. Leotard would stay head of the UDF.

Outgoing Education Minister Francois Bayrou agreed to head the UDF parliamentary group, indicating the loose-knit coalition had backed away from a break-up. He had said he wanted to establish a separate centrist group in the new parliament.
